meta.title: There Is Still No Silver Bullet
meta.author: gered

comments.author: emk
comments.text:
Maybe it's because I read way more Claude output than could possibly be healthy, but this writing style seems strangely familiar:


Hand the writing to a tool and what’s left is auditing someone else’s guesses against a mental model that has quietly stopped being fed. That’s a different job, a worse one, and the stopwatch noticed. Meanwhile the dashboards go up and to the right while the outcomes stand still. (The churn and duplication data pointing the same direction is a story I’ve already told, so I’ll spare you the recap.)


I see these verbal tics everywhere now. And I can't tell whether everyone is letting an LLM write for them, or whether some people have spent so much time reading slop that they've started speaking it natively.

Anyway, I think the author's point is basically valid. LLMs can help a lot with Brooks called "accident". But they help far less with "essence." It's not that they can't do essence at all. One of the reasons I find Fable a bit alarming is that up to a few thousand lines, it can do the essence, even for problems that involve enough odd constraints that no solution exists anywhere in the training data. But once a program becomes too big to fit in a context window, or a couple of sessions, the lack of hard thinking about the "essence" still becomes painfully noticeable.

But some of the people who are very happily succeeding with LLMs are people who only needed a couple of thousand of lines of code in the first place. There are a lot of problems in the world like that.

(I am currently engaged in industrial-scale deslopification of a successful prototype. I have bad news for all those people running "lights-out software factories": If they're not reading the code, then they have no idea what an absolute dumpster fire large-scale, unsupervised LLM code becomes. But since the people doing that won't listen, then I wish them fun with that.)

comments.author: darth-cheney
comments.text:
In today's computing world, "applications" -- whether they be online or on the computer -- are unfortunately siloed. It's been this way for a long time now. There was a lot more promise in the late 80s and 90s, where end user programming as a technique was taken quite seriously (I'm thinking of things like HyperCard, or how the desktop publishing industry made extensive use of AppleScript workflows).

This type of thing was abandoned because mainstream computing came to think it was not important. It was, it should be noted, also not that profitable. It's harder to sell little pieces of software if people can just stitch up a solution quickly.

I am not convinced things will change for the better when the purported solution is predicated on a trillion and a half dollars in investment looking for a return.

comments.author: darth-cheney
comments.text: Oh, let me be straight: the "naive LLM" solution to this problem is completely ridiculous. It's the total wrong way to go. The spirit of my comment was that the failure to properly implement end-user programming in the direction it was heading decades ago is, in part, to blame for the situation where regular people are trying to build apps this way

comments.author: ggpsv
comments.text:
Yes, I was referring to popular discourse.

I am conflicted because on one hand, I've seen first hand how excited non-technical folks are of coercing an LLM to build something practical that they would have otherwise not been able to do. They get to experience a myriad of feelings that we technical folks take for granted.

And yet, I perceive no understanding on their behalf of what's going on or what it means to maintain what's been conjured. Does it even matter though? Popular discourse is quick to dismiss this. I think it does matter. Any change to improve the software's fit depends yet again on rolling the dice and coercing the LLM to get you what you're after, sans regressions. What's worse is that rolling the dice can suddenly work differently, or become much more expensive. Suddenly, you may no longer coerce it to your liking.

Lastly, this technology can generate working systems so easily that you lose sight of their underlying complexity. The person got a working tool, but how well can they operate it in the long term? Are they better off than spending some time learning basic Python/SQL to build a simpler yet more robust tool that satisfies their needs?

comments.author: darth-cheney
comments.text:
All opinion of course, but I think first and foremost there needs to be a more humble recognition that computing environments are more relevant to this than are programming languages, and that there is not generally a better definition of "programming" other than "telling a computer what to do." Put those two together and the solution becomes apparent: you need to have a computing system whose layers can be peeled back like an onion, with different metaphors and abstractions at each layer. "Code" does not necessarily need to be involved at all of these layers, but the system needs to be as malleable as possible at each and every one of them.

Also let's disenthrall ourselves from the idea of "apps" or that anyone except system developers should need to make them -- "apps" as we understand them are isolated things with very few affordances for interacting with other "apps." If the computing system is made up of malleable computing materials, the boundaries between "apps" vanish (hints of this in the past: lisp machines, smallatalk environments, and, at a higher level, mandated applescript-ability, SK8, etc). What I have noticed consulting small organizations for years is that it is precisely these app boundaries that frustrate users: they don't want to build full scale "apps", but they want two or more apps to work together in a way that they currently do not, or they want one app to do just one slight thing that it cannot already do.
